Development of libraries in Australia  
A library is part of the experience of most Australians. Whether it is the school library, the local 
municipal library, a visit to an imposing State Library reading room, or a forage around the 
shelves of the bookmobile (a mobile library in a truck which services remote areas), a library is 
where we often ‘find out’. According to Brian Johns, at one time Managing Director of the 
Australian Broadcasting Corporation, ‘It is hard to imagine where we would be without libraries 
and without organised information; libraries are at the centre of our shared knowledge.’ 
 
When the 11 ships of the First Fleet arrived in Australia from England in 1788, they brought not 
only convicts, soldiers, plants and animals from Britain to the new colony of New South Wales, 
but also the colony’s first printing press and first books. These books were not those of a public 
library, but the small collections of individuals, or books of the type of learning thought to be 
necessary in the establishment of a new colony — law books, religious books, books of science 
and navigation. But as Peter Biskup points out in his book Libraries in Australia, the most 
important thing brought to Australia in the First Fleet which impacted on the development of 
libraries was the idea that libraries would be an important asset for the colony. 
 
The first, although unsuccessful, attempt to establish a public library in the new colony of New 
South Wales was through an appeal to the British public by the Reverend Samuel Marsden. In 
1809 he began to collect contributions so that he could set up a library of ‘carefully selected 
books … suited to the poor settlers employed in agriculture, the soldiers and the convicts’. 
 
In 1821 a catalogue of books in the personal libraries belonging to private citizens in the colony 
was compiled. From these, a number of libraries began to emerge. The 1820s saw the setting 
up of subscription libraries, where the user had to pay to borrow books, and by the 1830s the 
introduction of Schools of Arts, and Mechanics’ Institutes had further added to the number of 
libraries available to the people of the colony. The first of these in Australia was the Van 
Diemen’s Land Mechanics’ Institute, Hobart, which opened in that city in 1827. Others followed 
in Melbourne and other Australian cities and towns. By 1900 Australia supported 1,000 
Mechanics’ Institutes each with memberships of between 100 and 200 people. Most of these 
institutes had fewer than 1,000 books. 
 
The ‘School of Arts’ movement had begun in Britain in the beginning of the 19th century and 
produced a worldwide response. The first School of Arts opened in Edinburgh, Scotland in 1821, 
with others opening in Glasgow, Scotland and London, England in 1823. In Australia, the term 
‘Mechanics’ Institute’ was popular, but the institutions so named could also be known as 
Schools of Arts. These schools or institutes were places where people, mainly working class 
men, could go and hear lectures of use to them in their practical work, or access a library of 
books, and so improve themselves. Mechanics’ Institutes were very often supported by the 
colonial governments — usually by land grants and cash assistance. They were particularly

popular in country areas where their role often went far beyond their ‘library’ function to 
providing a general focus for the community’s cultural activities. Because of this important role 
and because of the support of the colonial governments, Mechanics’ Institute buildings were 
frequently quite imposing, and today form an important part of Australia’s built heritage. The 
Tenterfield School of Arts, Tenterfield, New South Wales, was the venue in which the statesman 
Henry Parkes made a famous speech, which is now seen as the first step towards the creation 
of the nation of Australia. 
 
Free municipal libraries began to appear in Australia in the 1850s, as did central public libraries 
— which largely went on to become the State Libraries. Parliamentary libraries were established 
to support the work of state parliaments, and a Commonwealth Parliamentary Library was set 
up in Melbourne in 1901 to support the new Commonwealth Parliament. In 1923 the 
Commonwealth Parliamentary Library became the Commonwealth National Library, the 
precursor to the National Library of Australia, which became a separate entity under its own Act 
of Parliament in 1960. 
 
Libraries today are much more than storehouses for books. Technologies like the internet mean 
libraries now also provide readers with gateways to the online world, and librarians are the 
finders of knowledge in cyber space as well as in their own stacks. The internet also makes the 
National Library of Australia’s heritage — the vast collection of books, manuscripts, photos, 
posters and leaflets — more accessible to more Australians. As the former Minister for 
Communications, Information Technology and the Arts, Senator Richard Alston stated, libraries 
are no longer simply storehouses of information and resources, but are actually gateways to 
information from all over the world.
